title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 32: Mirasol v. DPWH: Regulation of Traffic on Tollways
keywords: DPWH Administrative Order No. 1, Series of 1968
DPWH Department Order No. 74, Series of 1993
Revised Rules on Limited Access Facilities
There was no absolute right to drive
primary_topics: Chapter 32 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Mirasol v. DPWH, in which the Supreme Court, speaking through Justice Antonio T. Carpio, partly granted the petition and voided DPWH Department Orders 74, 215 and 123 for want of authority, while upholding Administrative Order No. 1 and with it the regulation of motorcycles on tollways.

The decisive question of agency power: because the functions of the old Department of Public Works and Communications were split by Presidential Decree 458 and Executive Orders 546 and 710, the authority to regulate limited-access facilities under Republic Act 2000 devolved to the DOTC and not to the DPWH, so the DPWH issuances and the Toll Regulatory Board rules resting on them were void.

The constitutional limits of the right to travel: AO 1, issued in 1968 while the old department still held the power, enjoyed the presumption of validity, passed the police-power test of reasonableness, and regulated only the mode of travel -- petitioners remained free to access the tollway.

Justice Dante O. Tinga's dissent, joined by three other justices, arguing that highway administration had always run through the Bureau of Public Highways to the DPWH and that the Court should have distinguished the power to regulate transportation (a DOTC prerogative) from the power to regulate highways (a DPWH one).
sub_topics: Pursuant to Republic Act 2000 (the Limited Access Highway Act), the DPWH issued Department Order No. 215 on June 25, 1998, declaring the Manila-Cavite (Coastal Road) Toll Expressway a limited-access facility.

Petitioners went to the Regional Trial Court of Makati to nullify AO 1 (1968), DO 74 (1993) and Article II, Section 3(a) of the 1998 Revised Rules on Limited Access Facilities promulgated through the Toll Regulatory Board, as inconsistent with Republic Act 2000.

The procedural history: the RTC's June 28, 2001 preliminary injunction against the total motorcycle ban on the North and South Luzon Expressways and the Coastal Road; the DPWH's July 18, 2001 DO 123 allowing motorcycles of 400 cubic centimeters displacement inside tollways; and the March 10, 2003 Decision that dismissed the petition yet struck DO 123 down as violative of the equal protection clause.
The three issues on appeal: res judicata, whether DO 74, DO 215 and the TRB regulations contravened Republic Act 2000, and whether AO 1 and DO 123 were unconstitutional.

First issue: the earlier injunction was a mere ancillary remedy, not a final determination, and Section 9 of Rule 58 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure required a final injunction to confirm it, so the Order did not bar the later dismissal of the petition.

Second issue and the history of the DPWH: from the Revised Administrative Code of 1917 through PD 458 (1974), the 1973 renaming of departments as ministries, EO 546 (1979) and EO 710 (1981), the Court traced the split and asked which of the two successor agencies could regulate limited-access facilities.

The holding on devolution: the authority to administer and enforce laws relative to transportation went to the DOTC, not the DPWH; hence DO 74 and DO 215 were void, the TRB could derive no rule-making power from the DPWH, and the implementing rules fell with them.
Third issue: DO 123 was voided simply for the DPWH's want of authority to promulgate it, so the Court never passed upon the equal-protection classification of motorcycles by engine displacement.

AO 1 valid: issued in February 1968 by the secretary of the then Department of Public Works and Communications under Section 3 of Republic Act 2000 -- before the split -- it had the force of law, enjoyed the presumption of validity, and was not oppressive since it merely set rules for public safety and traffic flow.

The right to travel did not include the right to choose one's vehicle: the mode of using a tollway could validly be limited by regulation, driving being a heavily regulated privilege rather than an absolute right.

The Tinga dissent, joined by Justices Azcuna, Chico-Nazario and Garcia: Republic Act 1192 had created the Bureau of Public Highways in 1954 under the old department, and it was that bureau -- with the chief highway engineer at its disposal -- that regulated limited-access facilities from 1957 onward.

The dissent's reading of the reorganizations: the Ministry of Public Highways continued to exist alongside the new ministries, so its powers were never transferred to Public Works or to Transportation and Communications, and EO 710 devolved them to the DPWH.

The dissent's institutional argument: the DOTC exercised land-transportation authority through the LTO (registration, licensing, traffic adjudication), the Land Transportation and Traffic Code said nothing about limited-access facilities, and the Administrative Code referred highway matters to the DPWH.

The dissent's closing appeal: the DPWH had traditionally established and regulated limited-access facilities without objection from other agencies, and judicial deference should be accorded that long-standing practice absent an unequivocal conferment of authority on the DOTC.

notable_anecdotes: The motorcycle concession: three weeks after the trial court enjoined the total ban, the DPWH issued DO 123 on July 18, 2001 admitting motorcycles of 400 cubic centimeters displacement into the tollways -- an accommodation the Supreme Court later voided for want of authority.

The trial court's reversal of itself: the same RTC that had granted petitioners their injunction in 2001 dismissed their petition in 2003, while declaring the DPWH's own concession, DO 123, unconstitutional under the equal protection clause.

The genealogy of a department: the digest walks from the seven executive departments of the 1917 Revised Administrative Code through PD 458, the 1973 renaming of departments as ministries, EO 546 and EO 710, in order to answer the question of which of the two successor agencies was now authorized.

The dissent's appeal to practice: Justice Tinga observed that the DPWH had always established and regulated limited-access facilities to the exclusion of and without objection from other agencies, the DOTC included, and asked that judicial imprimatur be granted to that practice.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 32 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Mirasol v. DPWH, the tollway-traffic case decided for the Court by Justice Antonio T. Carpio. Acting under Republic Act 2000, the Limited Access Highway Act of 1957, the DPWH had issued Department Order No. 215 in June 1998 declaring the Manila-Cavite (Coastal Road) Toll Expressway a limited-access facility, and petitioners sued in the Makati Regional Trial Court to nullify that order together with Administrative Order No. 1 of 1968, Department Order No. 74 of 1993 and the Revised Rules on Limited Access Facilities promulgated through the Toll Regulatory Board. After the trial court enjoined the total motorcycle ban in June 2001, the DPWH issued DO 123 admitting motorcycles of 400 cubic centimeters, and in 2003 the same court dismissed the petition while voiding DO 123 on equal-protection grounds. On appeal the Court partly granted the petition. It first held that the earlier injunction was a provisional remedy that merely served to preserve the status quo, an ancillary measure that Section 9 of Rule 58 required to be confirmed by a final injunction, so res judicata did not bar the dismissal. It then traced the old Department of Public Works and Communications through Presidential Decree 458, the 1973 renaming of departments as ministries, and Executive Orders 546 and 710, concluding that the authority to regulate limited-access highways devolved to the Department of Transportation and Communications; DO 74, DO 215, the TRB regulations and DO 123 were therefore void, and the equal-protection question was never reached. AO 1, however, had been issued in 1968 before the split, enjoyed the presumption of validity and merely set rules to ensure public safety and the uninhibited flow of traffic; the right to travel did not mean the right to choose any vehicle in traversing a tollway, there being no absolute right to drive. Justice Tinga, joined by three colleagues, dissented, tracing highway administration through the Bureau of Public Highways to the DPWH and urging deference to long-standing practice.
